headline: Your cartilage
body: A working circadian clock inside the tissue, running without your brain.

headline: Isolated tissue
body: Growth plate cartilage in organ cultured femurs runs a measurable circadian clock. No brain attached, no light input, no feeding cues. The tissue oscillates on its own.
punch: Disconnected from the body and still on schedule.

headline: PTH
body: Parathyroid hormone signalling resets the circadian clock specifically within cartilage. A hormone that already regulates the growth plate also carries timing information into it.
punch: One pathway doing regulation and scheduling at once.

headline: Which matters
body: PTHrP sits in the feedback loop with Indian hedgehog that controls when chondrocytes stop proliferating and start hypertrophy. That's the loop deciding how long cells keep dividing.
punch: The timing signal plugs into the growth decision.

headline: Clock genes
body: Circadian machinery in cartilage gates matrix production, proliferation and metabolic activity across the day. These aren't background rhythms, they're the tissue's actual work being scheduled.
punch: Cartilage does different jobs at different hours.

headline: Which is why
body: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses, biggest during deep sleep. A tissue running its own clock is set up to be more responsive at some points in that cycle than others.

headline: What's established
body: The clock exists in cartilage and PTH resets it. Whether disrupted sleep measurably changes adult height in humans has not been tested.

headline: The usable point
body: Hormone effects here depend on when the signal arrives, not only how much arrives. That's already proven for GH, where pulsatile delivery beat continuous at matched dose.
punch: Amount and timing are separate variables.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
